chapter_title: A Catechumen asked the Apostle: When I would give
spiritual_reading:
A matter of spiritual order may be understood by comparing two kinds of interaction with the human mind and life.

There is a state in which malice and opposition act first. One who is in hostile will assaults another in the first degree of life and injures what should have remained whole. Afterwards he attacks again, not content with the first harm, but presses the injury further, renewing it and intensifying it, so that what was already damaged becomes a standing testimony in the life of the injured. When this is brought into the light of discernment, the harmed one appeals to what judges justly in the interior. Then the examining faculty turns directly upon the injurer and searches the quality and origin of the injury that remains as a fixed trace in the life. The falsity and violence are laid open as though the very power of understanding were shattered. The matter is then led into spiritual judgement; a sentence is formed according to the ruling love. Retribution is permitted in the same kind as the harm, so that evil returns into the evil’s own form and the injurer experiences the measure he imposed; and because he struck one who had not yet acted from such hostility toward him, the injury is increased to the extent of that unjust beginning. The opposition is not set aside, because judgement follows the quality of enmity itself.

After this process reaches its end, that hostile will is condemned because it acted from retaliation and set itself in sin against the other. But there is another state that can appear similar outwardly while being opposite inwardly. The one who was harmed is afterward brought into a condition of spiritual weakness; the injury manifests as an active disorder in the life, and he becomes distressed because falsity and evil now work within what was opened. He therefore turns to one who has skill in restoring, and he reveals the disorder. Yet the restoring agent does not proceed from hatred or from the intent to harm. He applies keen truth to the disordered state and separates what is corrupt from what may be saved. When this is done, interior truth is released with force; the person is in pain, yet he receives it because he perceives the end. No retaliation is in it, nor is injustice imposed, because the act is for the sake of restoration. Everything done is from good as the ruling purpose, not from evil as the direct intention.

When the work is completed, the disorder is opened, what must be removed is cast out, and the life is made sound. Gratitude then flows, and acknowledgment is given. That former distress and the restoration become a testimony to the restoring wisdom; the one who heals is held in honour because the use is seen.

So it is with this whole matter in the presence of the living principle in a person. When truth first touches what is disordered, it seems like a blow; yet if it is from the intent to set in order, it is good, and rest is provided afterward. From such restoration there arises a glory for the healing work itself, even though in the moment of separation and correction it is painful.

But there is also the other kind: one who attacks the companion in the community of life from cruelty and contempt for what is living within. He acts from a will that delights in injury, and he justifies himself by opposition. Over such a state the accusation stands, because it is not correction for good but assault from evil.

fills.notes: The enemy strikes again and then continues the assault; the substrate needs a verb of furthering the injury before repeating ‘hits over his blows’.
Corresponds to ‘renewing and intensifying’ the prior harm: he ‘hits over his blows’ and renews them.
Introduces the repeated blows as a definite set already mentioned.
Marks the sores as the specific standing marks left by the assault.
The narrative requires the harmed party to become the subject who goes to judgement and makes the accusation before the judge.
The judge examines not merely the fact but the nature and origin of the marks; ‘quality’ matches the correspondential emphasis on state.
Judgement is rendered according to the form of enmity; ‘in this way’ links the retaliation rule to the principle stated after it.
Condemnation is for retaliation and for establishing sin against the other; the lacuna likely joins the two causes.
The victim becomes sick afterward; ‘again’ signals a subsequent state after the first judgement sequence.
The disorder manifests from the opened injury; the wound ‘comes out on him’ from that source.
In the spiritual sense he turns to one skilled in restoring; in the natural figure he ‘seeks help’ before calling the doctor.
The doctor is distinguished by lacking hostile will; ‘no enmity’ matches the opposition between malice and healing use.
Pairs naturally with ‘nor …’; the doctor has neither retaliatory intent nor harmful purpose.
After healing, the gratitude and honour are directed to the doctor: ‘He shall even make him gifts…’.
The matter is about corrective action that seems like harm but is restoration; ‘matter of healing’ fits the ensuing explanation.
Introduces the application: ‘It is at the time…’.
Spiritual logic demands the moment when ordering truth touches the disordered life, appearing as a blow.
Sets up the apparent injury: it ‘seems as though you have struck…’.
Object is the living soul/living principle spoken of in the paragraph.
Rest and ease follow correction; the temporal sequence is essential in the correspondence.
Joins ‘it is well’ to the resulting rest.
Matches ‘ease shall exist for it’; rest is the correspondential outcome of order restored.
Links the immediate pain to the later settled state.
‘Glory’ belongs to the use itself: the work of healing/restoration, not to assault.
Holds the paradox: glory and good end, yet present pain during separation and correction.
The ‘other person’ here is the opposite kind: not healer but hostile striker; ‘enemy’ keeps the correspondence with cruelty and contempt.
The comrade belongs to the community of life; the assault is ‘sick with his’ cruelty, i.e., a diseased will acting upon the living principle.
The motive is cruelty in the spiritual sense; the natural figure needs the named cause of the striking.
Envy is a common substrate form of hostile opposition to life in another; it fits ‘he being cruel according to …’.
Supplies the continued assault upon the living soul, matching the parallel with repeated striking earlier.
Natural idiom for violent action; spiritually it corresponds to willful assault rather than corrective incision.
Introduces the standing charge that follows.
The conclusion is that the accusation stands because the act is from evil opposition, not healing use; ‘enmity’ names that ruling state.

assessment: Most gaps can be restored to a coherent oldest-layer comparison between hostile retaliation and corrective healing, because the correspondential structure tightly constrains sequence (assault → judgement → retribution; then disorder → physician → incision → bleeding → healing → honour; then the contrary case of cruelty). Exact connective particles and some naturalistic idioms in ¶7–¶8 remain less tightly constrained, so several fills there are tentative even though the underlying spiritual functions are clear.
